title: Irma P. Hall, ‘Soul Food’ and ‘The Ladykillers’ actor who found fame at 60, dies at 91
content: Irma P. Hall, the veteran actor who brought warmth and authority to matriarchal roles in “Soul Food” and “The Ladykillers,” and whose acting career took off after decades as a teacher, died Tuesday in Dallas. She was 91. Her family announced her death Wednesday. No cause was given. Hall was best known to many viewers as Big Mama, the family’s steadying force in the 1997 film “Soul Food.” The role earned her an NAACP Image Award and led to a return as the character in the television series based on the film. She received a Cannes Film Festival Jury Prize for her performance as Marva Munson, a Bible-reading landlady opposite Tom Hanks in the Coen brothers’ 2004 comedy “The Ladykillers.” Hall also appeared in “A Family Thing,” “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil,” “Beloved,” “Patch Adams,” “Collateral” and Tyler Perry’s “Meet the Browns.” Hall was 60 when “A Family Thing” brought her a major film role. She played Aunt T., a blind woman whose counsel helps guide two half brothers, played by James Earl Jones and Robert Duvall. The part drew attention to an actor who had spent years developing her craft onstage and in smaller screen roles. “I was just concentrating on developing this craft,” Hall said in a 1996 interview with The Associated Press. “I guess you really never know where you are, you probably think you are on a lower rung than you really are.” Hall had not set out to become an actor. Born Irma Dolores Player on June 3, 1935, in Beaumont, Texas, she was raised in Chicago and later returned to Texas for college. She taught English and foreign languages in Dallas public schools for more than two decades. Her path to the screen began when actor and director Raymond St. Jacques heard her recite poetry in Dallas and cast her in his 1973 film “Book of Numbers.” Hall continued teaching as she took acting roles, then made performance her full-time work in the 1980s. She also helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre and remained involved in developing young artists. Hall’s career included theater, television and film. Her credits ranged from the 1997 Clint Eastwood drama “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil” to the 1998 films “Beloved” and “Patch Adams.” She also voiced Great Aunt T. in the 2001 “Rugrats” Kwanzaa special. In 2004, Hall was recovering from serious injuries suffered in a car crash, including open-heart surgery, a broken arm and a crushed ankle, when she traveled from a Chicago convalescent center to attend a private screening of “The Ladykillers.” “I loved the whole thing,” she told The Associated Press. “You never really know until you see it on the screen.” Hall said she had heard from Hanks and the Coen brothers while recuperating. They had signed her pillow, she said. “Whenever I miss them, I hug it.” In Dallas, Hall was also a longtime member and Church Mother at Inspiring Body of Christ Church. Her family remembered her as a woman of faith who read to children at the church’s school and stayed active in its theater ministry. “She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said in the family’s announcement.

title: Stacy Keach, star of stage and ‘Mike Hammer’ series, dies at 85
content: Stacy Keach, one of America’s finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85. Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, “after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure,” his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017. Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane. Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating “World’s Most Amazing Videos” on TV. He played a deranged colonel in “The Ninth Configuration” (also known as “Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane”), led the TV show “Titus” and had a role in Alexander Payne’s Oscar-nominated drama “Nebraska.” Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney’s bitter father in “Jay Kelly.” “My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career,” he told New York magazine in 2012. “My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I’ve gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything.” He played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries “Mistral’s Daughter,” a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz’s novel “Princess Daisy,” Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli’s “Jesus of Nazareth” and Maj. Jonas Steele in “The Blue and the Gray.” He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds. Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play “Indians,” played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in “King Lear” on Broadway and had other onstage roles there in “The Kentucky Cycle” in 1993, “The Country Wife” in 1965 and “Other Desert Cities” in 2011. He also headed the national touring company cast of “Frost/Nixon,” portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with “Sleuth” with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of “King Lear” at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for “Pamplona,” a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run’s cancellation. While he was still doing “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer” (later titled “The New Mike Hammer”), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London’s Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary. “As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats,” he wrote in his 2013 book, “All in All: An Actor’s Life On and Off the Stage.” He added: “It was the lowest moment of my life.” He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book “The Blue and the Gray.” The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months. In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, “The Long Riders.” He said the experience was “very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity.” After prison, he narrated the TV documentary “High on the Job,” and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. “There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one’s existence,” he testified. Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centers. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the “Hammer” series. He said he treasured her photos and letters behind bars. Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina. His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, “Intimate Strangers” with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, “The Return of Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” also played well, and then the “Mike Hammer” series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS’ 1986-87 schedule. Many years later, in the TV series “Prison Break” that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves. Born in Savannah, Georgia, Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art. In the summer of 1963, he worked with the Oregon Shakespeare Festival and played Henry V, Mercutio and Lord Berowne. He attended the Yale School of Drama and, in the summer of 1964, played several roles at New York’s Public Theater in “Hamlet” with Julie Harris. He went to study at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art as a Fulbright scholar and returned to New York to do various stage roles. Keach made his film debut in 1968 in “The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter” and played stoner cop Sergeant Stedenko from the Cheech and Chong movies. He worked for director John Huston twice, in “Fat City” and “The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean” and had roles in “American History X” with Edward Norton and “The Bourne Legacy.” He played a tough trucker in “Roadgames,” was electrocuted in “Children of the Corn” and a robot removed his heart in “Class of 1999.” His biggest break, though, came with the role of Hammer, whom he played as a modern-day knight, a champion of the underdog. “Keach makes a dashing, dapper Hammer. He looks almost jaunty in his tilted gray fedora,” said Fred Rothenberg, a TV writer for The Associated Press, in 1983. “He knows how to speak lust with his eyes, and talk dirty with his fists.”

title: 2026 was the year of tennis star Alexandra Eala – and she brings a nation with her
content: Hues of royal blue, red, white, and yellow flashed at every corner of the tennis court as the crowd rallied around Alexandra Eala. For a sport constantly looking for the next generational icon, Eala has become a unifying touchstone for an archipelagic nation of over 110 million people – with many of them scattered across the globe. The left-handed Filipina player had a whirlwind breakout season after defeating several top women’s stars. She ousted defending Wimbledon title holder Iga Świątek in the third round of the grass court major this summer. In August, she then beat Jessica Pegula in the Washington Open to become the first player from the Philippines to win a WTA Tour singles title . Eala started this year as world No. 53. She’s now ranked 15th, a career-high after she made the final at the Prudential Hong Kong Tennis Open in her last tournament of the season. The distinction means the 21-year-old is now the highest-ranked Filipino player and Southeast Asian in WTA history. The Filipino talent has already shown she can beat some of the sport’s biggest names, but with every new game, set and match on tour, it is inevitably harder to stay at the top. “I think that the expectation rises, but so does the demand in terms of what the sport demands of you and what the level demands of you,” Eala told CNN Sports. Though she very well may still be asking herself if she can be among the greatest in the sport, Eala knows she’s working towards that consistency and getting better. “I just look forward to having another season full of hardship, full of joy, and hopefully full of success,” she said with pensive confidence. Though her bid for another WTA title fell short in Hong Kong, the loss has done little to dim her breakout year. “This season has changed my life,” Eala told the crowd as tears welled up following her loss to Claire Liu in the Hong Kong Open final. “It has changed my life for the better. I am incredibly proud of the work we have put in this year. We are the only ones who truly knew what it took to arrive at this point in our journey.” Eala and Liu had found themselves locked in a fierce, early back-and-forth at Victoria Park in Hong Kong, but the 26-year-old American soon switched gears and took control – at one point winning nine consecutive games – to seal a 6-3, 6-0 victory in an hour and 33 minutes to claim her first-ever WTA title. “I can’t speak for everyone, but playing against Alex is one of the hardest things because of the crowd. No matter where she goes, she always has so many supporters, which I think is really great in general for tennis,” Liu said in a post-tournament presser. Wherever she played, Filipino fans have clamored for tickets to cheer Eala on, bringing a sense of home to a life spent traveling the global tennis circuit. Eala’s growing popularity has even seen her swing from the tennis court to haute couture. In September, the Filipino phenom sat front row alongside Anna Wintour at New York Fashion Week’s Michael Kors and Tory Burch shows. Tennis courts transform into homecoming celebrations when Eala makes an appearance. And it was no exception in Hong Kong, which is home to over 200,000 Filipinos, many of them who work as Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs). “We idolize her for her resilience, same as an OFWs who never give up,” Lids Romero, a domestic worker who spent her only day off on Sunday to watch the final at the official fan zone, told CNN Sports . Moy Volante, who flew in with his family from the Philippines to watch the tournament, told CNN Sports he admired Eala’s determination to push through, even in tough battles, which he hopes his daughter can embody. “You can really feel the unity and support of Filipinos,” Volante said of the atmosphere throughout the week. “I love their passion,” Eala said fondly of her fans. “They really support me without fail in so many tournaments.” Crowds of Filipino domestic workers, young professionals and school children all came out to Causeway Bay to watch Eala in action, even as her matches stretched late into the night over a regular school week. Young female fans were all over Victoria Park with some holding placards proclaiming, “Let’s Go! Alex” at the fan zone, while others in the stands waved colorful, hand-drawn banners. “I want them to get inspiration from Alex,” Marlon Avines who was at the park with his three daughters, said to CNN Sports. “The grit, persistence and giving pride to the country.” Eala has encouraged girls and young women who look up to her “to pursue whatever makes them happy.” “I think it’s better to go through the hardships doing what you love, and you can always come back to that when things get difficult,” Eala told CNN Sports. The young, rising star is no stranger to hardships. She began training in tennis as a preschooler, coached by her late grandfather, who she affectionately calls “Lolo Bob.” What started as a family pastime soon grew into a relentless pursuit, which Eala once described on Maria Sharapova’s podcast as an obsession like having a “crush on perfection.” In 2018, as a 12-year-old wild card, she won Les Petits As – a tournament widely considered to be the preeminent under-14 competition in the world – in the process becoming a talent to watch. A few months later – after turning 13 – she left Manila for Mallorca to train at the Rafa Nadal Academy in Spain on a scholarship. Eala began to flourish on the international junior circuit, winning her first junior grand slam title at the 2020 Australian Open in girls’ doubles. Just two years later, she became the first Filipina to lift a junior grand slam singles trophy at the US Open in 2022. Along with that junior success, she officially turned pro in March 2020. While Eala’s stature in the sport grows, what remains the same is the standard of discipline she sets for herself. “I’ve learned to push my limits,” Eala told CNN Sports. “I’ve learned a lot about what my limits are … and the bar can always be raised.”

title: African writing award probe finds 'no evidence' winning story was AI generated
content:
The Caine Prize for African Writing has said that after an internal review it has found no evidence that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza had used generative AI to write his winning short story and confirmed him as the winner of this year's £10,000 ($13,000) award.
Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, said the matter had been investigated following an article in US magazine The Atlantic with the headline, Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI.
"From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human written," she said in a video posted on X.
The accusation had caused a social media uproar and Kundizeza had denied the allegation.
The Atlantic article by journalist Vauhini Vara alleged that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.
Her allegations followed rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies .
Following the publication of her article last month, Vara had told BBC's Front Row programme that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".
The backlash on social media included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.
Wakatama said the Caine Prize organisation had considered Vara's allegations "carefully and fairly".
"We chose to take a human-centred approach to the investigation. Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel, and the Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published," she said.
"It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author."
In a statement, the Caine Prize explained further that the analysis had been conducted by an independent cyber security and digital forensic investigator .
The day after winning the prestigious Caine Prize award earlier in October, Kundizeza had told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.
He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.

title: Author says there were 'real concerns' about David Walliams within publishing industry
content:
Author Chloe Combi has said she had heard rumours that there were "real concerns" about David Walliams's behaviour within the publishing industry more than a decade ago.
Combi told BBC News she had heard there were allegations about his "behaviour around young female staff" and says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking".
An investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that Walliams has been accused by several women of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his position, which he denies.
HarperCollins, which published Walliams's best-selling children's books, dropped Walliams last year after an investigation into his behaviour.
In response to the Guardian and ITV report, a spokesperson for HarperCollins said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that it took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously".
Walliams told ITV News and the Guardian that he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.
At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams.
"We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said.
"She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."
Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained.
"One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."
Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."
Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".
HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.
The allegations against Walliams include:
In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.
"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."
He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."
Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".

title: Former BBC radio presenter Kelly dies aged 69
content:
Danny Kelly worked for the BBC until 2007
Former BBC radio presenter Danny Kelly has been described as a "broadcasting titan" following his death at the age of 69.
Kelly stepped back from his long-term role at Talksport after being diagnosed with throat cancer in March.
He presented a radio sports show on BBC London before joining Talksport in 2007 and was previously editor of the New Musical Express and Q magazine.
Talksport paid tribute to him on Wednesday, calling him a "much-loved friend" and a "broadcasting titan".
"A true legend of the station, Danny had time for everyone and went out of his way to be kind," they said. , external
"His genuine warmth and incredible passion for broadcasting will be sorely missed by all of us."
They added: "A cherished part of Talksport for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves.
"His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him."
Kelly also presented BBC radio shows in the 1990s with Danny Baker, who described him as a "great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew".
Kelly was a lifelong Tottenham fan and the Premier League club said he was "one of our own".
A club statement , external added: "Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Danny."
BBC Radio 5 Live's George Cummins was a friend and former colleague of Kelly at Talksport.
"Danny had an extraordinary knowledge of music and football," he said. "His ability to combine the two on air made him an incredible broadcaster.
"His brilliant wit made him an amazing story teller. Colleagues would often remark that his brain was like an encyclopaedia.
"While he was a genius on-air, it was his personality off-air that would shine through. He was always there to give advice and help. He always took an interest in colleagues' lives away from work.
"He was a very positive man. He loved his job. He loved entertaining the nation. I'll always remember a great friend who taught me so much."

title: 'A hell of a thing to take on': The moving inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while dying of Aids
content:
Oscar-tipped film Elsinore centres on the Chariots of Fire star's final acting feat before his death aged 40. Those closest to him then recall his extraordinary swansong.
Shakespeare's Hamlet famously stands as one of the most, if not the most, challenging theatrical parts in the English language. The play of the same name is Shakespeare's longest and the eponymous character has more lines than any other Shakespearean character by a considerable margin. But while countless illustrious actors have committed to playing the Prince of Denmark over the centuries, no one has done it in such extraordinary circumstances as Ian Charleson.
In 1989, he played the role at London's National Theatre to rave reviews as he was dying of Aids. It was an incredible feat of resilience that is now being retold in the biographical film Elsinore, named after the castle in which Hamlet is set. It has left critics and early viewers deeply moved – in particular by the performance as Charleson of Andrew Scott, who is now favourite to win next year's best actor Oscar.
Charleson was most famous for playing Eric Liddell , the devout Christian athlete who refused to race on Sundays, in the Oscar-winning 1981 hit Chariots of Fire. He was in another Oscar-winner, Gandhi, the following year.
However by 1989, the Scottish actor was dissatisfied with his career. So when the opportunity arose to play what is widely considered the greatest Shakespearean role on the greatest British stage, the vast Olivier stage at London's National Theatre, he was determined to defy the ravages of a terrible terminal illness in order to take it.
Charleson wasn't the first actor to play the Danish prince in the production. Elsinore opens in the National Theatre on Tuesday 5 September, 1989, with his predecessor in the role, Daniel Day-Lewis, fleeing the stage during Act 1 Scene 5, when Hamlet is confronted by the ghost of his murdered father. After that, Day-Lewis could not be persuaded to return.
This certainly happened, although a mythology has grown up around the incident. For years the story was that Day-Lewis had seen the ghost of his own father, the poet Cecil Day-Lewis, on stage. The actor himself claimed as much although in an interview in 2012 he clarified that he had been speaking metaphorically.
It was always the plan that Charleson would take over from Day-Lewis, having been offered the role earlier that year by director Richard Eyre. Charleson was in Eyre's 1982 production of Guys and Dolls, and the director thought very highly of him.
In fact, Charleson had already played Hamlet twice. Firstly, in Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead at London's Young Vic theatre and then in a touring production of Shakespeare’s play in 1974. But he was unhappy with his performance in the latter.
Third time round, he knew he wasn’t going to get another chance. By this time, Charleson, who had been HIV positive since 1986, had developed Aids, the most advanced stage of the infection. His close friend Sean Mathias, a theatre and film director played in the film by Matthew Beard, was among the few who knew. Mathias didn't think Charleson should play Hamlet.
"It is probably the biggest role a male actor can play," Mathias tells the BBC. "It's a hell of a thing to take on for any actor because your mind's got to go to a very dark, complex place and you've got to make these extraordinary connections between life and death.
"Then there's the physicality of the thing – you're on stage for perhaps four hours, giving mammoth monologues. I was just really worried it would precipitate his illness."
Charleson was being treated by Margaret Johnson, a young respiratory physician who had been tasked with setting up an HIV service at the Royal Free Hospital in Hampstead, London. When she first met the actor, she had no idea who he was.
"I remember asking him, as I asked all patients, how he was coping and whether he had any financial problems," Johnson tells the BBC. Charleson let the concerned doctor know he was comfortably off, having cut a deal for Chariots of Fire which gave him a percentage of the profits.
In the film's version of Johnson, played by Olivia Colman, she is not thrilled about Charleson playing Hamlet. While she doesn’t expressly forbid him, it's clear she thinks such a demanding engagement is at odds with his efforts to stay healthy. In reality, Johnson had a very different approach. "I'm not someone who would ever have said to him to even consider not doing Hamlet," she says. "I would never say don’t get on with your life. I always had the view 'Who knows what’s going to happen? Let’s hope things improve'."
She says Colman in the film is very unlike her: "She comes over as a much more senior, bossy person, which I certainly wasn't. I was a very young and probably pretty naive doctor." But, she accepts that a certain amount of "poetic license" is inevitable.
When Charleson first began rehearsing with the company after Day-Lewis's sudden departure, the story was put about that he was recovering from a sinus operation, to account for his poor health. But eventually he decided, as is depicted in one of Elsinore's most moving scenes, to tell his fellow actors the truth. One by one in the film, they come up to hug him or shake his hand.
"I'd worked with Ian previously and as far as I recall, I knew he had Aids before he made his announcement to the assembled company," says Paul Jesson, who played Horatio. "That happened much as portrayed in the film and everyone was completely supportive."
Charleson gave his first performance on October 9. His face was often so swollen that it was difficult to see his eyes – the official line given to the press was still that he was recovering from an operation. Jesson says: "Andrew Scott's performance is magnificent, deeply affecting. He brilliantly embodies Ian Charleson and there were times when I thought he was Ian. The only thing I would say, and it's hardly a criticism, is that Ian was physically so much weaker than in Andrew's portrayal. He would rely on me literally to support him and by the end of a performance he hardly had the strength to lift the sword, let alone fight the duel."
Johnson recalls: "On a couple of occasions I had to ring Richard Eyre for him, when he didn't feel well enough to do it. He'd ring me and he'd say 'Please would you call him, I can't bear it'."

title: Littler expected 'pub players' on Netflix show
content:
Luke Litter was beaten by Fallon Sherrock after defeating 14 prior challengers
Luke Littler has admitted he thought he would be facing pub players on his recent Netflix show, which was billed as giving "amateurs a chance at life-changing money".
Broadcast live globally on the streaming platform last month, the cash was won by top women's player Fallon Sherrock.
The format of 'Beat Luke Littler' saw 24 players selected to take on the world number one in a single leg of 501, hoping to win a prize of Â£501,000.
The 24-strong field did include low-level opponents, such as an Australian jockey, a bin man and a Nando's manager, but anyone who was not a member of the PDC Tour was also allowed to compete.
That meant Sherrock - who became the first female player to beat a male opponent at the PDC World Championship on her way to the last 32 in December 2019 - and leading junior players Mitchell Lawrie and Zach Griffiths were also eligible.
"Before I saw the line-up, I thought it was just pub players," said Littler, who is preparing for the Grand Slam of Darts this weekend.
"Whereas obviously when the line-up came out, I probably knew just over half of them.
"Mitchell, Zach Griffiths - I played with him on the Development Tour - obviously Fallon, Katie Sheldon and a lot more.
"I mean Fallon, she's never had a Tour card, so she went for the qualifiers and she made it through. But then she wasn't guaranteed to play - she went in on a vote."
Sherrock, who has been awarded an MBE for her services to darts, made it through an audition process and then had to rely on the public to select her to take on Littler at Manchester Central.
Littler beat 14 contestants but then lost to Sherrock, who won nearest the bull to throw first and then checked out in 15 darts.
"It was a very good night overall," Littler added. "I think from my side it was very good. From Netflix's side, it was very good.
"I think the whole thing was probably a learning curve. For me, constantly playing back-to-back, especially in the heat, I was going off and on stage. I'm up for another one and I'm sure Netflix will be as well.
"There aren't many people who could say they've got their own show, and I've had my own show on Netflix, which is just still bonkers to me."

title: Wayne Rooney leads I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! line-up
content:
Former England and Manchester United footballer Wayne Rooney, Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page and YouTuber Sharky will be among the intrepid crew entering the jungle Down Under for this year's I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!
They will be joined by Kaiser Chiefs frontman Ricky Wilson, Paralympian and presenter Ade Adepitan, actress Claire Sweeney and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.
TV presenter AJ  Odudu, comedian Jack Skipper, Love Island contestant Chloe Burrows and model Leomie Anderson round out the team headed for Australia.
Hosts Ant and Dec will return with the ITV show's opening episode on Monday, 16 November, with the series now in its 26th year.
Rooney is following in the footsteps of his wife Coleen, who was runner-up on I'm A Celebrity in 2024.
"If you're going in you want to win it," he said. "Coleen's already tried and obviously she finished second in the show so I'm here to bring that title back to the Rooney household."
Rooney admitted that jumping out of a helicopter is his biggest fear. "I've been booked to jump out of a plane three times before and never made it on the plane," he said.
"I don't like snakes or what is in the water either - I don't go in the sea."
Producers are making adaptations to the Australian jungle camp so it is accessible for Adepitan.
In a press statement, he said: "For me, this is a moment in time. Even if I go out in the first week, I will always be remembered as the person in a wheelchair. I am slightly overwhelmed. It's never been done before, and it never crossed my mind I would be the first."
Keith Lemon comedian Leigh Francis is not among the official line-up but is rumoured to become a late addition.
The last I'm A Celebrity series was the all-star version in South Africa, which was marked by heated arguments and walk-outs among the cast during the live final in April.

title: Police helped remove Russell Brand after 'violent incident' at Jemima Goldsmith's home
content:
Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident took place.
Thames Valley Police said officers were contacted by an alleged victim and went to an address in Oxfordshire on 25 July 2014 but no arrests were made.
They listened to her concerns and gave support, and "also ensured the victim's partner left the address, as per the victim's wishes", the police added in a statement on Wednesday.
Goldsmith, who dated Brand for about a year, wrote on X on Monday that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.
Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault on Monday.
In her post, 52-year-old Goldsmith, who wasn't part of the trial, said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".
She wrote: "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse.
"I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident."
The Press Association reported that Goldsmith had asked for Brand to leave the property, her wish was then communicated to him by police, and he agreed to leave the house.
Goldsmith added: "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.
"I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."
She also said she had "assisted the journalists who finally exposed him", and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" if they were sued.
TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

title: Jonathan Ross 'horrified' by Walliams allegations and Brand conviction
content:
TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is "horrified" by allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams and the rape conviction of Russell Brand.
In a statement, Ross said he was once "on friendly terms with both men", but that at the time he was "genuinely unaware of their conduct".
ITV News and the Guardian on Tuesday published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. Walliams denies all the allegations against him. Brand was sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape on Monday.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said that the allegations against Walliams were the "latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the media.
Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers, or allege other inappropriate behaviour.
In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
In his statement, Ross also addressed a joke he made at a comedy awards show in 2004, in which the punchline suggested Walliams would be "going home" with a 15-year-old.
Ross acknowledged the controversial quip and described it as "tasteless".
He added: "This joke was submitted to me by the Comedy Awards script writing team and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect.
"Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him."
Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliams and Russell Brand.
He said he was "as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation".
He added: "My thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."
The allegations include:
In the ITV documentary revealing the allegations, Jonathan Ross is pictured at an event also attended by a woman who later made accusations about the conduct of Walliams.
Ross and Brand were also widely criticised for leaving lewd voicemails for Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs, the grandfather of Georgina Baillie with whom Brand was in a consensual relationship in the mid-2000s, during a BBC Radio 2 broadcast.
Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years' imprisonment for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and the Metropolitan Police has confirmed several people have approached them about the disgraced star since his conviction.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said on Tuesday: "These allegations are the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power in an industry where we have known for so long that the power imbalances are huge.
"Russell Brand's eventual conviction was a stark reminder that we are still far too reliant on the courage of brave women who choose to come forward despite knowing they will pay a heavy price and may not be believed - and a handful of persistent journalists who risk everything to tell their stories.

title: Armand Van Helden and Faithless to play Ayr's Pavilion dance festival
content:
House music legend Armand Van Helden, DJ duo CamelPhat and dance pioneers Faithless are among acts lined up for the fifth year of a popular Ayrshire music festival in 2027.
Pavilion Festival co-founder Ewan McVicar will top the bill on Saturday 1 May alongside CamelPhat, the Liverpool pair who have enjoyed hits like Cola and Panic Room in the past.
Van Helden, who has had a career spanning 40 years, will then headline on Sunday 2 May, with organisers expecting about 18,000 fans to attend.
The event was created by McVicar and Scottish promoter Ricky Magowan. Past performers have included Carl Cox, award-winning DJ Ben Hemsley and Madchester group the Happy Mondays.
McVicar said the past few years of the event have "been a wild ride", born from wanting to bring something back to Ayr.
He added: "Ricky and I wanted to bring something special to Ayr, and seeing people come back with their pals every year is what makes it. We've got some incredible names joining us in May, with plenty more still to announce.
"Playing in your home town is always special, but celebrating five years of your own festival there is something else."
In October McVicar completed his debut Club Knuckles residency at the Hï Ibiza nightclub, having performed there every Friday from May onwards.
The Pavillion event will boast four outdoor stages and a weatherproof Big Top main stage.
Organisers said Van Helden, the producer behind 90s chart-topping hit You Don't Know Me, will perform a headline set celebrating house music's enduring connection with Scottish dancefloors.
Faithless and Groove Armada are also confirmed for DJ sets over the weekend, bringing names synonymous with big hits like Insomnia, God Is a DJ and Superstylin to the bill.
Other acts announced so far include Ultra Naté, DART and Kyle Starkey, with the rest of the line-up due to be confirmed in the coming months.

title: Huge mural celebrates Stoke-on-Trent's clubbing heritage
content:
Work has begun on a large mural celebrating Stoke-on-Trent's clubbing heritage.
Two former DJs, Phil Johnson and Bob Leigh, wanted to pay tribute to the city's venues and its DJs and raised £11,000 needed for the project.
Local artist Tom Edwards, who has been tasked with creating the work, said it had been a difficult process finalising the design, as there had been so many suggestions of stories and themes from the large community the pair had created.
The artwork is being painted onto the side of a bar on Adventure Place, Hanley, and he is aiming to complete it by mid-December.
It nods to a range of local clubs from across the decades, including The Golden Torch , The Place , The Void and Maxims, as well as DJs like Keith Minshull, Trevor M, Dave Evison and Pete Bromley .
In 2025, Leigh and Johnson installed blue plaques at sites where historic venues and nightclubs once stood.
Leigh said the "tremendous response" to the plaques inspired the mural. They announced plans for the 5m (16ft) by 25m (82ft) artwork in January.
The initial plan was to produce a series of small paintings to go next to the plaques. Instead, they decided "to go big or go home," Leigh said.
"It's been a long time coming, this has, for various reasons, and the past few months have been very fraught. But we've got Tom, so we're winning."
Edwards' work can already be seen across the city. He is best known for wildlife murals, the most recent of which is on the Trent and Mersey Canal near Stoke railway station.
The latest project had stood out as "something a bit different from what I normally do and a really cool project to get behind".

title: What's in store now the Big Burns Supper is no more?
content:
Plans for a three-day "winter extravaganza" in Dumfries have been unveiled following the demise of the Big Burns Supper (BBS) festival.
Organisers admitted the old format - which brought big name artists to the town for more than a decade - was "never really sustainable".
In its place is an entirely free Dumfries and Galloway Carnival programme from 29 to 31 January with light installations, music and hundreds of community performers.
Executive producer Graham Main said they were aware money was tight for many people and he hoped the new format was right for the town and the region as a whole.
The first BBS took place in 2012 and was made up of 80 events covering music, dance, comedy, theatre and art across 40 different venues.
Acts ranging from Nina Nesbitt to the Undertones and Black Grape to the Bay City Rollers would come to perform and, within a few years, it was a nine-day event.
However, after the Covid pandemic, it struggled to recover and was cancelled in 2024 after it failed to secure funding from EventScotland.
It returned but organisers confirmed earlier this year that it was the end of the road for the festival in the format that brought the Spiegeltent venue to town.
Main told BBC Scotland News: "It never really was sustainable, if I'm being perfectly honest.
"Even up until the pandemic, whilst the public might have experienced world class culture, we were very honest about the fact that it never quite broke even."
He said they had learned during Covid to "think outside the box" and he believed they had done so again with their new plans.
"I think what we have always been very good at is trying to tune into what feels right for right now," he said.
"And we are taking a temperature reading and we don't think people have got that much money after Christmas.
"So, therefore, actually what's more important to us is bringing people back together to connect."
Main said they hoped to bring the same "magical energy" as before - just presented in a different way.
"I think what we've done is we've sort of used the abundant resources which we have - which is empty shops and derelict buildings on our High Street," he added.
"I think we've tried to turn that into a positive because what we've done with Northern Lights is really utilise those empty spaces."
The event includes three days of live music, a winter village in the town centre and street traders.
A parade - which attracted thousands of people this year - will return in 2027 with lanterns being made across the south west of Scotland
"There are few times we actually come together as a region, even in football, you know, we're split between various towns," said Main.

title: Author says there were 'real concerns' about David Walliams within publishing industry
content:
Author Chloe Combi has said she had heard rumours that there were "real concerns" about David Walliams's behaviour within the publishing industry more than a decade ago.
Combi told BBC News she had heard there were allegations about his "behaviour around young female staff" and says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking".
An investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that Walliams has been accused by several women of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his position, which he denies.
HarperCollins, which published Walliams's best-selling children's books, dropped Walliams last year after an investigation into his behaviour.
In response to the Guardian and ITV report, a spokesperson for HarperCollins said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that it took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously".
Walliams told ITV News and the Guardian that he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.
At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams.
"We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said.
"She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."
Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained.
"One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."
Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."
Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".
HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.
The allegations against Walliams include:
In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.
"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."
He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."
Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".

title: Crime drama is not portrayal of city I want to see, says mayor
content:
A mayor has said he would like TV dramas set in his home city to focus on the "warmth" of the people, rather than "drugs, organised crime and criminal activity".
Steve Rotheram, the metro mayor of the Liverpool city region, said he had just finished watching the second series of BBC One drama This City is Ours, which follows the fortunes of the fictional Phelan crime family, and is filmed across the area and in Spain.
Rotheram said the drama was "brilliant" and praised its "cinematic, film-like" quality and "top-notch" acting.
But he said that "overall" it was not a portrayal of his home city that he wanted to see, adding he felt characters were often reduced to negative stereotypes.
Last month, stars of the crime drama defended it against claims it showed the city in a negative light and glamourised a life of crime.
Earlier this year, acclaimed Liverpool-born producer Jimmy Mulville questioned whether a focus on crime drama shaped the city's wider reputation , and whether it reflected the reality of life in Liverpool.
Crime dramas set in the city have proved extremely popular, and have provided a platform for local storytellers such as Tony Schumacher - who created The Responder - to reach a wide audience.
The first series of This City is Ours generated around £9m for the local economy, according to the Liverpool City Region Combined Authority.
The production spent around 17 weeks filming during 2024, and generated or sustained about 300 jobs and introduced about 17 apprentices to the film industry, according to an impact report by the Liverpool Film Office.
Rotheram said: "We need to get away from the drugs and crime and organised crime and criminal activity to what most people are renowned for, which is the warmth of their welcome, their friendliness, their humour.
"And that's what really the Liverpool City region is about for me."
He added he thought "some of the Scouse accents were a bit dodgy".

title: Toby Jones stars in film about UK Mars mission
content:
Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".
Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.
The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.
Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."
Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.
Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.
His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.
The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.
Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.
The director added: "Joe Bone's beautiful script has made it easy to attract some of the best names in the business to join our brilliantly creative team and I'm thrilled to be working once again with my friend Toby Jones."
Crook, known for his roles in The Office and Pirates of the Caribbean, previously worked with Jones on Detectorists , the BBC's Bafta-winning comedy he wrote, directed and starred in.
He also starred in Small Prophets, a comedy which made its debut on BBC Two and the BBC iPlayer in February.
The film is expected to be released in 2027.

title: 'You makes Barry proud' - Gavin & Stacey star Joanna Page to enter I'm a Celeb jungle
content:
Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page has confirmed she will appear on the upcoming reality TV series I'm a Celebrity, with her former co-star Ruth Jones urging her to "have a crackin' time".
Page, who played Stacey Shipman in the BBC comedy, is joining this year's line-up of celebrities on the forthcoming show in Australia.
The 49-year-old, from Swansea, said she had her sights on becoming the first Welsh Queen of the Jungle.
"You makes Barry very proud, I'm not gonna lie," said Jones - assuming her former Gavin & Stacey character Nessa Jenkins - on Instagram.
"They're gonna make you stick all manner of matter in your gob. And I'm not talking Gwen's omelettes... Just don't over do it, alrigh'? You knows what a weak constitution you has."
Speaking ahead of her trip down under, Page said she believed her co-stars will be "shocked" when she arrives in the jungle for the ITV reality show.
"I also know they will find it funny. They know exactly what I am like and they will laugh."
Page said being the first Welsh queen would be a "pretty good title to take home", but added she was just as excited to see how long she could last.
"I'm not going to crumble," she said.
"I'm going to see this to the end and I'm going to be strong. I am going to get the most out of this."
As a mother-of-four, Page said she hoped her part in the show will help her "reconnect" with who she was before becoming a mum.
"This is a once-in-a-lifetime experience. I'm very much an impulsive person and I just make a gut decision, so I said 'yes' straight away," said Page.
She said she hoped to find "peace and time for my thoughts" away from the everyday worries about feeding the children and getting everyone ready for the school run.
"I can be me, I can be Jo and not just mummy all the time. I think that will be nice."
"I will never get to do anything like this again. I am telling myself, 'Come on Jo, let's take yourself off to Australia and give yourself an experience'.
"It's exciting and it's going to be life-changing."
Page will enter the jungle alongside footballer Wayne Rooney, TV personality Chloe Burrows and soap star Claire Sweeney.
Rooney will follow in his wife Coleen's footsteps after she finished as runner-up on the 2024 series, and said he hoped "people will see me for who I am".
He said he had "always wanted to do" the show, joking that because of his short-lived football managerial career, he had more time on his hands.
"I like to have fun and I like to think I am actually a fun guy to be around.

title: 'A hell of a thing to take on': The moving inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while dying of Aids
content:
Oscar-tipped film Elsinore centres on the Chariots of Fire star's final acting feat before his death aged 40. Those closest to him then recall his extraordinary swansong.
Shakespeare's Hamlet famously stands as one of the most, if not the most, challenging theatrical parts in the English language. The play of the same name is Shakespeare's longest and the eponymous character has more lines than any other Shakespearean character by a considerable margin. But while countless illustrious actors have committed to playing the Prince of Denmark over the centuries, no one has done it in such extraordinary circumstances as Ian Charleson.
In 1989, he played the role at London's National Theatre to rave reviews as he was dying of Aids. It was an incredible feat of resilience that is now being retold in the biographical film Elsinore, named after the castle in which Hamlet is set. It has left critics and early viewers deeply moved – in particular by the performance as Charleson of Andrew Scott, who is now favourite to win next year's best actor Oscar.
Charleson was most famous for playing Eric Liddell , the devout Christian athlete who refused to race on Sundays, in the Oscar-winning 1981 hit Chariots of Fire. He was in another Oscar-winner, Gandhi, the following year.
However by 1989, the Scottish actor was dissatisfied with his career. So when the opportunity arose to play what is widely considered the greatest Shakespearean role on the greatest British stage, the vast Olivier stage at London's National Theatre, he was determined to defy the ravages of a terrible terminal illness in order to take it.
Charleson wasn't the first actor to play the Danish prince in the production. Elsinore opens in the National Theatre on Tuesday 5 September, 1989, with his predecessor in the role, Daniel Day-Lewis, fleeing the stage during Act 1 Scene 5, when Hamlet is confronted by the ghost of his murdered father. After that, Day-Lewis could not be persuaded to return.
This certainly happened, although a mythology has grown up around the incident. For years the story was that Day-Lewis had seen the ghost of his own father, the poet Cecil Day-Lewis, on stage. The actor himself claimed as much although in an interview in 2012 he clarified that he had been speaking metaphorically.
It was always the plan that Charleson would take over from Day-Lewis, having been offered the role earlier that year by director Richard Eyre. Charleson was in Eyre's 1982 production of Guys and Dolls, and the director thought very highly of him.
In fact, Charleson had already played Hamlet twice. Firstly, in Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead at London's Young Vic theatre and then in a touring production of Shakespeare’s play in 1974. But he was unhappy with his performance in the latter.
Third time round, he knew he wasn’t going to get another chance. By this time, Charleson, who had been HIV positive since 1986, had developed Aids, the most advanced stage of the infection. His close friend Sean Mathias, a theatre and film director played in the film by Matthew Beard, was among the few who knew. Mathias didn't think Charleson should play Hamlet.
"It is probably the biggest role a male actor can play," Mathias tells the BBC. "It's a hell of a thing to take on for any actor because your mind's got to go to a very dark, complex place and you've got to make these extraordinary connections between life and death.
"Then there's the physicality of the thing – you're on stage for perhaps four hours, giving mammoth monologues. I was just really worried it would precipitate his illness."
Charleson was being treated by Margaret Johnson, a young respiratory physician who had been tasked with setting up an HIV service at the Royal Free Hospital in Hampstead, London. When she first met the actor, she had no idea who he was.
"I remember asking him, as I asked all patients, how he was coping and whether he had any financial problems," Johnson tells the BBC. Charleson let the concerned doctor know he was comfortably off, having cut a deal for Chariots of Fire which gave him a percentage of the profits.
In the film's version of Johnson, played by Olivia Colman, she is not thrilled about Charleson playing Hamlet. While she doesn’t expressly forbid him, it's clear she thinks such a demanding engagement is at odds with his efforts to stay healthy. In reality, Johnson had a very different approach. "I'm not someone who would ever have said to him to even consider not doing Hamlet," she says. "I would never say don’t get on with your life. I always had the view 'Who knows what’s going to happen? Let’s hope things improve'."
She says Colman in the film is very unlike her: "She comes over as a much more senior, bossy person, which I certainly wasn't. I was a very young and probably pretty naive doctor." But, she accepts that a certain amount of "poetic license" is inevitable.
When Charleson first began rehearsing with the company after Day-Lewis's sudden departure, the story was put about that he was recovering from a sinus operation, to account for his poor health. But eventually he decided, as is depicted in one of Elsinore's most moving scenes, to tell his fellow actors the truth. One by one in the film, they come up to hug him or shake his hand.
"I'd worked with Ian previously and as far as I recall, I knew he had Aids before he made his announcement to the assembled company," says Paul Jesson, who played Horatio. "That happened much as portrayed in the film and everyone was completely supportive."
Charleson gave his first performance on October 9. His face was often so swollen that it was difficult to see his eyes – the official line given to the press was still that he was recovering from an operation. Jesson says: "Andrew Scott's performance is magnificent, deeply affecting. He brilliantly embodies Ian Charleson and there were times when I thought he was Ian. The only thing I would say, and it's hardly a criticism, is that Ian was physically so much weaker than in Andrew's portrayal. He would rely on me literally to support him and by the end of a performance he hardly had the strength to lift the sword, let alone fight the duel."
Johnson recalls: "On a couple of occasions I had to ring Richard Eyre for him, when he didn't feel well enough to do it. He'd ring me and he'd say 'Please would you call him, I can't bear it'."

title: Wayne Rooney leads I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! line-up
content:
Former England and Manchester United footballer Wayne Rooney, Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page and YouTuber Sharky will be among the intrepid crew entering the jungle Down Under for this year's I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!
They will be joined by Kaiser Chiefs frontman Ricky Wilson, Paralympian and presenter Ade Adepitan, actress Claire Sweeney and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.
TV presenter AJ  Odudu, comedian Jack Skipper, Love Island contestant Chloe Burrows and model Leomie Anderson round out the team headed for Australia.
Hosts Ant and Dec will return with the ITV show's opening episode on Monday, 16 November, with the series now in its 26th year.
Rooney is following in the footsteps of his wife Coleen, who was runner-up on I'm A Celebrity in 2024.
"If you're going in you want to win it," he said. "Coleen's already tried and obviously she finished second in the show so I'm here to bring that title back to the Rooney household."
Rooney admitted that jumping out of a helicopter is his biggest fear. "I've been booked to jump out of a plane three times before and never made it on the plane," he said.
"I don't like snakes or what is in the water either - I don't go in the sea."
Producers are making adaptations to the Australian jungle camp so it is accessible for Adepitan.
In a press statement, he said: "For me, this is a moment in time. Even if I go out in the first week, I will always be remembered as the person in a wheelchair. I am slightly overwhelmed. It's never been done before, and it never crossed my mind I would be the first."
Keith Lemon comedian Leigh Francis is not among the official line-up but is rumoured to become a late addition.
The last I'm A Celebrity series was the all-star version in South Africa, which was marked by heated arguments and walk-outs among the cast during the live final in April.

title: New push to turn island into screen destination
content:
The film industry is calling for the creation of a new commission to make it easier for productions to shoot in Jersey.
Filmmakers, politicians and investors met at the Jersey Screen Summit on Monday to discuss developing a sustainable film and television industry.
It was organised by director Rebecca Coley as a way to get government and film sector representatives "on the same page" and she said the creation of a commission would "be a one port of call for all productions happening here".
Assistant Economic Development Minister Senator Serena Kirsten said the government was looking at options to support the industry but added further talks were needed to get it "right".
Coley said a film commission could help producers deal with the island's layers of governments including the parish system.
"They could liaise with all the different departments because it is quite confusing as an outsider understanding all our parishes and who to speak to for all the different elements that you need for filming," she said.
"That's what they have in most other places in the world where filming takes place, one central office takes care of all the permits and deals with all the different departments to help make it smooth sailing while the production happens."
She acknowledged that one of the biggest barriers to attracting productions was the cost of filming on island.
"All the other jurisdictions where filmmaking takes place have incentives like a cash rebate or a tax incentive ," she said.
"At the moment, because Jersey doesn't have any of those things that's why we haven't seen more productions here.
"I think because Jersey needs to diversify its economy, let's give this a chance."
Brian Constantine, executive producer of the reboot of the TV show Bergerac, said the series had shown what was possible in terms of developing the industry.
While parts of the series are filmed in Jersey, filming has also taken place in the UK.
"Money is a really big thing," he said.
"There are inherently much larger costs coming to Jersey at the moment. For example we're putting up a hundred people every time we come here - that's a huge amount of the budget that we wouldn't necessarily be spending if we were using UK crews."
He said creating a film commission would be a "one stop shop" for anyone wanting to film the island.
"They'll be able to tell you what you can do, what you can't do, all the things that you don't think about when you're watching a TV show," he said.
"We've been able to demonstrate that we can make a television show that sells around the world in little old Jersey and Jersey can compete in the right environment on that world stage."
Samantha Perahia, head of production at the British Film Commission, said Jersey already had the building blocks of a successful industry.
She said the island had an "abundance" of locations but she added cast, crew and facilities were needed to support production.

title: How to visit key Rivals locations from new series
content:
Filming locations that feature in the popular TV series Rivals are once again putting the West of England "on the map" as the second season of the Disney+ drama hits our screens.
The series, based on one of the late Dame Jilly Cooper's so-called bonkbusters, features an all-star cast including Aidan Turner, David Tennant and Danny Dyer.
Filming for series two happened in places such as Bristol Harbourside, Corsham in Wiltshire, Berkeley Castle in Gloucestershire and Ammerdown House in Somerset, with towns across the region standing in for the Cotswolds and London.
Matt Booker runs The Corsham Toy Shop and said it was a "bonus" to have Rivals filmed there and brought in trade.
Bristol provided the backdrop for several key scenes in the hit drama, with locations across the city transformed to recreate the fictional county of Rutshire.
The private Bottle Yard Studios' TBY2 facility in Hengrove was used for a number of interior sets, including the offices of Corinium TV, interiors of The Priory and an authentic-looking 1980s television control room.
You can visit Aerospace Bristol in Filton which provided the setting for scenes involving supersonic jets and Concorde, while the Bristol Marriott Royal Hotel featured as a location for character stays and social gatherings.
The show also utilised Corn Street, Queen Square and Denmark Street as the backdrop of 1980s London, with period vehicles, including Sinclair C5s, helping to recreate the look and feel of the decade.
Plus, you can wander along the city's harbourside, where Canon's Wharf and Harbour Hotel were used for TV awards scenes and those set at Sansovino Hall.
Other familiar locations include the Cosy Club Bristol restaurant and Bristol Hippodrome.
In Wiltshire, you can amble along the historic high street of Corsham, used extensively as the primary filming location for the fictional town of Cotchester.
Imagine the streets lined with classic cars and shops having had their fronts tweaked to take the market town back to the 1980s.
Boots was turned into an old-fashioned Waitrose, the town hall was transformed into a polling station and the Royal Oak pub was transformed into Bar Sinister.
Booker said: "Tourists come and find where things were filmed and take photos."
Jeweller Daisy Coppin said it had been "really exciting" to see the town so vibrant.
Two miles south is the Grade II* Listed Neston Park, used as Tony Baddingham's estate, The Falconry.
The historic 18th-Century country house is not open to the public, however you can walk around the village of Neston and its Recreation Ground.
Just a stone's throw away in Chippenham, Georgian listed manor house Langley Park was used to portray various pool parties in the series. Although it is a luxury hotel and events venue, its grounds connect to popular hiking trails.
Gloucestershire has been a filming spot for Rivals since its first season, with Chavenage House in Tetbury being used as the set for the O'Hara family home, The Priory.
Guided tours and visits of the 16th-Century Elizabethan manor are by reservation only.

title: Jonathan Ross 'horrified' by Walliams allegations and Brand conviction
content:
TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is "horrified" by allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams and the rape conviction of Russell Brand.
In a statement, Ross said he was once "on friendly terms with both men", but that at the time he was "genuinely unaware of their conduct".
ITV News and the Guardian on Tuesday published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. Walliams denies all the allegations against him. Brand was sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape on Monday.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said that the allegations against Walliams were the "latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the media.
Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers, or allege other inappropriate behaviour.
In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
In his statement, Ross also addressed a joke he made at a comedy awards show in 2004, in which the punchline suggested Walliams would be "going home" with a 15-year-old.
Ross acknowledged the controversial quip and described it as "tasteless".
He added: "This joke was submitted to me by the Comedy Awards script writing team and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect.
"Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him."
Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliams and Russell Brand.
He said he was "as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation".
He added: "My thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."
The allegations include:
In the ITV documentary revealing the allegations, Jonathan Ross is pictured at an event also attended by a woman who later made accusations about the conduct of Walliams.
Ross and Brand were also widely criticised for leaving lewd voicemails for Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs, the grandfather of Georgina Baillie with whom Brand was in a consensual relationship in the mid-2000s, during a BBC Radio 2 broadcast.
Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years' imprisonment for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and the Metropolitan Police has confirmed several people have approached them about the disgraced star since his conviction.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said on Tuesday: "These allegations are the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power in an industry where we have known for so long that the power imbalances are huge.
"Russell Brand's eventual conviction was a stark reminder that we are still far too reliant on the courage of brave women who choose to come forward despite knowing they will pay a heavy price and may not be believed - and a handful of persistent journalists who risk everything to tell their stories.
